newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Slovenia new favourite to win NATO place.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia new favourite to win NATO place.

text.p: Slovenia has emerged as the best placed outsider to win NATO membership when the alliance expands later this year, and Romania is unlikely to squeeze in despite a strong lobbying campaign by France, alliance sources say.

NATO countries, which are planning to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance at a summit in July, are keen to send a signal to other former Yugoslav republics of the rewards in store if the Balkans remain peaceful.
"One of the arguments of those in favour of enlargement is that it spreads stability, taking in Slovenia strengthens that argument," said one military source.
Support has recently swung behind Slovenia because of the West's desire to show enlargement is more than just granting membership to former enemies in the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.

In sharp contrast to Croatia and Serbia, Slovenia has clearly brought its small military under civilian control and adopted constitutional reforms protecting democratic opposition -- key conditions for NATO and European Union membership.
"Slovenia in many ways meets many of the criteria many people are looking at," said Simon Lunn, deputy secretary-general of the North Atlantic Assembly, NATO's parliamentary arm.
Lunn and other independent analysts also stress the strategic attraction to military planners of Slovenia providing a land link between Hungary and Italy.

NATO sources said Romania is unlikely to be one of the first new entrants for two decades even though France has come out publicly in favour of Bucharest being rewarded for wide-ranging economic and military reforms.

"France wants Romania to be part of the first wave in the NATO enlargement. I want to reassess France's support for Romania in the process of joining the alliance," French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier told reporters on Tuesday.
Speaking in Bucharest, he said Romania's geographic location and political stability should qualify it for membership.

But military sources at the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) say Romania is unlikely to be make it despite Paris's advocacy and the fact it has scored top marks in all the military tasks demanded by existing alliance members.
"Economically, it is not up to it," said one source.
NATO sources say leaving out Romania could create problems for the Western allies by throwing the spotlight on how countries qualify for membership.
"It makes clear the issue is essentially political and reopens the debate on the cost of enlargement," said one diplomat.
Enlargement has recently emerged as one of the main foreign policy planks of the second administration of President Bill Clinton.

But with estimates of its cost fluctuating widely from $30-80 billion more and more people are openly questioning its necessity -- particularly at a time when Russia poses no threat to central and eastern Europe.
